Part I: Diversifying AI ownership

Diversifying AI ownership

Hauke Hillebrandt

Abstract

What if everyone owned a little bit more of everything? Here, we argue that we should diversify the ownership of corporations to reduce risks from AI.

In Part 1, we highlight three benefits of diversification:

  1. Power becomes decentralized, reducing risks from malevolent actors.
  2. Actors developing TAI have fewer incentives to profit from negative externalities.
  3. Greater global collaboration and less adversarialism in TAI development.

We believe diversification is tractable, as diversification both:

  1. Hedges against risks to the domestic economy and technological unemployment

And:

  1. Increases the expected returns of investors

In Part 2, we propose concrete policies that diversify the ownership of corporations.

All countries should:

  1. Create sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) and pension funds that passively invest in the global market portfolio.
  2. Create tax incentives to invest in the global market portfolio and reduce distortions and disincentives from doing so.
  3. Improve corporate taxation through self-assessed taxes.

We close with a series of drawbacks, risks, and reservations of these policies.

Part I: The benefits of increasing common ownership

  1. Decentralizing Power & Increased Global Collaboration

International tensions have put strains on collaboration within AI safety research,[1] which could lead to coordination failures. We must cooperate to successfully reduce many different global risks,[2] and rising national-security-based regulations AI[3] suggest that AI is not safe by default. Here we argue that more diversification of ownership of corporations can help reduce global risks, especially risks from transformative AI.

Currently, power over AI is very concentrated:

  1. In a few countries: Especially in the US and China, with only some important suppliers of chips in Taiwan and the EU.[4] 
  2. In a few corporations: Frontier AI firms Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI (SpaceX), Facebook (Meta). Nvidia is the main producer of AI chips and now the world’s biggest corporation. Perhaps some Chinese corporations (e.g. Tencent). [5],[6]
  3. Few key people have outsized control (e.g. Google and FB’s founders have voting control through super-voting shares despite owning only ~10% of shares, Elon Musk owns roughly 60% of xAI).
  4. Few players have outsized ownership: while Google, Meta, Nvidia, Amazon are all only ~⅔ commonly owned by institutional investors (e.g. Blackrock, Vanguard, etc.), Tencent is only half owned by institutional investors.

And AI could be a winner-takes-all industry that might concentrate even further (cf. Big Tech has bought more AI startups recently e.g. SpaceX has bought Cursor).[7] These power concentration incentives trap AI firms in a zero-sum 'race to the bottom', sacrificing AI safety for speed.[8]

By increasing diversification, we decrease the concentration of ownership. In turn, greater common ownership disincentivizes exploiting negative externalities (e.g. risks from AI uplift) for profit.

To illustrate, imagine a Big Tech firm with just one shareholder — call him Elon. Suppose Elon has total control and a substantial stake of the firm. The firm aims to maximize shareholder value, a lot of which is value-to-Elon. However, Elon's actions may affect Alice, who has no say in the firm's decisions and a much smaller stake. As the number of shareholders increases (say, to include both Elon, Alice and the rest of the world), the closer 'maximizing shareholder value' approaches 'maximizing value-to-everyone', rather than just 'value-to-Elon'. Both profits and negative externalities get shared more widely, and so diversification leads to fewer advantages to profit from untaxed externalities. In particular, diversification reduces the incentive to produce (global) public bads (e.g. risks from unsafe AGI).

As we diversify and the number of shareholders gets larger, i.e. as we converge on full common ownership, corporations become more and more incentivised to approximate acting on the interests of all. And so, the more we mutualize corporations, the more we reward safety and transparency,[9] and decrease adversarialism between competing AI firms.

Diversified ownership increases collaboration, as up- and downsides of AI become more widely shared.[10] The more we diversify, the larger our stakes in foreign firms, which incentivise us to collaborate and not support adversarial policies or arms races. If one company or country gets ahead, we are less incentivized to war. This is why trading partners go to war less often.[11] Similar benefits from diversification apply to other public goods.

Put simply, generally, the more globally integrated our world economy becomes, the more incentive we have to coordinate to reduce global risk that would affect everyone vs. local risks that only affect us domestically.

Conventional Economic Benefits

Diversification is feasible and economically beneficial. Contrary to optimal portfolio theory, many investors show "home bias" by holding excessive domestic assets. [12] Home bias is a 'robust stylised fact'[13], 'too large and widespread'[14] across many countries to be due to chance.[15] Though information effects may partially explain home bias[16], evidence indicates it's also irrational,[17] and reducing it will boost returns.[18]

The more strongly markets of different countries correlate, the less beneficial it is to diversify.[19] But even if one considers market correlations, domestic investment is inefficient.[20],[21] Further, local investment bias is to be expected given 'distance-based' models of investment decisions, which also explains a variety of international data in developed markets.[22] US investor home bias is returning, indicated by decreasing international market correlations.[23] Inefficient diversification exists despite minimal US economic home bias, because investors do not invest optimally across foreign countries, even if there is no obvious home-country-specific bias.[24] Investors may even irrationally underestimate the most impactful tail risks, leading to yet greater inefficiency.[25] In sum, inefficient diversification in many countries stems from home bias. 

diversifying more leads to moral hazard: the less home bias, the less invested a country is in itself, and the less it is incentivized to produce more.[26] (cf the incentives of the CEO of Tesla, whose shares can increase by hundreds of billions a year, to those Volkswagen, who earned a mere $10M—100,000x less because he owns a much smaller stake in VW).[27] But the difference between current and optimal levels of diversification are stark and seemingly random: Empirically, in the US, efficiency loss is ~112b/year[28] or ~1% of GDP, [29],[30], and in France, it’s ~$33b/year or ~2% of GDP.[31] This has substantial implications for the macroeconomy.[32]

Hedging against risks and technological unemployment

Global labor compensation is approximately $60T per year.[33] Even if diversifying would not yield higher financial returns in expectation, hedging against risks from TAI, in particular labor displacements (‘technological unemployment’), might still increase expected utility. If AI does well, more people will profit, but if it doesn’t do well, current returns to labour will remain high.

Risks from events that have never happened before (like AGI) are underinsured.[34] Diversification insures and hedges against such risks, particularly against technological unemployment, where AI has a transformative global impact before it can do all tasks humans can do.[35] This could cause super-exponential economic growth,[36] or be otherwise transformative (e.g. drastically increase income inequality[37] or a large lead by one country or company could lead to a stable, perpetual global totalitarianism).

The more we diversify, the more we benefit from our competitors' success: either we get financially compensated,[38] or we can use our increased resources to outcompete potentially malevolent (or even just self-interested) actors.[39] 

Effects on differential technological development

Dilemma: The more directly we invest in AI startups, the more we speed up AI (ETFs of publicly traded AI firms vs. GMT) and the more governments are involved in picking winners. But the more diversified the portfolio, the less effective the hedge. If we were to invest directly into AI labs, then they would  subsidize AI development, which might speed up AI.

And so we might want to invest in either just publicly traded AI companies or in the global market portfolio, which now has substantial exposure to the AI sector.

Current state of diversification

A large part of the AI sector are publicly traded via two channels:

  1. Indirectly: Publicly traded companies either have their own frontier AI efforts or have substantial stakes in newer frontier AI firms (e.g. Microsoft owns a substantial stake of OpenAI,[40] Google owns DeepMind and has a stake in Anthropic.[41]Amazon, SK Telecom own substantial stakes in Anthropic. [42] Meta is publicly traded.
  2. Frontier AI companies: SpaceX has now gone public and owns xAI and Cursor. Anthropic and OpenAI might have their IPOs in 2026.

Such common ownership can have anti-competitive effects and reduce innovation.[43] Recently, institutional investors have pressured Big Tech to spend less on 'moonshot R&D'.[44] But when large investors own technologically related firms it mitigates this problem as their firms act in their interest and can profit by innovating via R&D as a 'public good to their competitors' that might otherwise be unprofitable.[45] When technology spillovers are relatively large, an increase from the 25th to the 75th percentile of common ownership is associated with an increase of +13% in citation-weighted patents.[46]

Sovereign Wealth Funds to diversify AI ownership

!! noah smith’s phd supervisor Why the US needs its own sovereign wealth fund 

Socialists like it too: Matt Bruenig, “On Piketty's Capital: The Sovereign Wealth Fund Solution.” | Basic Income News 

Lead, Own, Share: Sovereign Wealth Funds for Transformative AI | Convergence Analysis 

To diversify AI ownership, we propose that countries set up sovereign wealth funds (SWFs) which passively invest a fixed fraction of GDP in the global market portfolio.

SWFs guard against external risk,[52] and allow us to reap the benefits of diversification. SWFs '[protect] the income of future generations' because they can transform 'concentrated exposure of public assets to volatile commodity prices into a more balanced and diversified global exposure'.[53]

Countries should passively invest in the global market portfolio for steady long-term returns, rather than relying on the state to outperform the market.[54] The more nations invest in the global market portfolio, the greater their stake in the success of the global economy and leads to more global coordination, fewer externalities, and insurance against centralization of power.[55] 

By investing passively, we minimise politicization, where SWFs 'selectively [buy] control in entities due to narrow nationalistic objectives'.[56] As there is no active fund management, the administrative costs are trivial.[57] Despite claims that active investment by SWFs offers no benefit, outperforming passive benchmarks remains challenging.[58] 

SWFs are politically tractable, because:

  1. Creating SWFs is in a country's financial interest.

We believe this both because of the conventional economic benefits from diversification listed earlier, and the success of extant SWFs. In addition:

  1. There is growing interest in both SWFs, and unconventional foreign reserves investment strategies.

Many SWFs already exist, and there is burgeoning interest from the EU, who are considering a €100bn investment in a tech-focused SWF,[59],[60] (though it proposes to only buy shares in European tech companies[61]). SWFs already have traction, both in practical discussions and in popular policy proposals. For instance, some have promoted SWFs as a means of financing a universal basic income.[62] More broadly, the US Fed has bought corporate bond ETFs in 2020,[63] [64] some of which include foreign firms.[65] 

Finally, we note that:

  1. SWFs allow countries to benefit from AI, without directly investing in AI.

Directly investing in AI might cause political brouhaha, as firms worry about nation-states influencing foreign AI development. This could occur even if nation-states buy non-voting shares, as other avenues of influence still remain. By suggesting investment in the GMP, we mitigate concerns of selective influence. Despite this, nation-states retain influence in worlds where there is a large degree of centralized power, so long as SWFs approximate the GMP at any given point in time.

While conditional dividend payouts provide the best incentives against premature liquidation, our proposal could be made revenue-neutral. For instance, revenue from the SWF could be used to cut taxes.

2. Pension policy and homeownership

Households are buying ever more ETFs. This trend, spurred by the popularization of Modern Portfolio Theory, the pursuit of lower investment fees, and legislative changes such as the U.S. Pension Protection Act of 2006, has channeled trillions of dollars into the hands of a few large asset managers.

We should reduce many of the subsidies and tax incentives for homeownership, which disincentivizes international diversification, because subsidies for homeownership subsidize domestic assets (E.g. US homeownership is subsidized by ~$100B annually [66] [67]).  Many are either regressive or ineffective in increasing homeownership rates[68] (e.g. the US home interest mortgage deduction [69] and the UK's 'Help to Buy' scheme.) a[70] and excessive homeownership rates might increase unemployment and NIMBYism.

Homeownership subsidies should be replaced by tax cuts to incentivise savings (e.g. UK’s stocks and shares ISA scheme). Individuals should be entitled to automatic opt-out tax cuts for investment into internationally diversified pension funds.[71]
Subsidizing internationally diversified funds is a modest change, as most Western governments already subsidize retirement saving. Few households adjust their default pension plan despite policy changes.[72] Households which do make adjustments are disproportionately wealthier and more financially sophisticated.[73] By aligning the default pension plan with global growth, we provide the poorest with more wealth in retirement.

Pensions would be an effective way to increase investment in the global market portfolio and increase diversification. Take Germany, which already has an even higher net international investment position (NIIP) as a percentage of GDP than any other Western European country, even if they have a higher GDP per capita.[74] German households' current levels of stock ownership, German households own ~0.66% of the global economy. If policy changes drove German stock ownership to US levels, then German households would own ~1.4% of the total global economy through stock holdings.[75] For Germany alone would amount to ~$1T in more diversification.

“The country is the world’s largest foreign creditor. Its net international investment position—overseas assets held by Japanese owners, minus Japanese assets held by overseas owners—runs to $3.5T, far north of China’s $2T. This huge pile is the result of decades of high savings.”[76]

Tax policy

Digital Sales Taxes

The EU has proposed new rules for taxing digital business profits in member states.[80] The proposal has majority support among economists,[81] and already has widespread EU uptake.[82] Revenue generated via digital sales taxes should be used to hedge against AI risk. Given the source of the income, campaigns to use such revenue for SWF investment (aimed to hedge against AI risks) could be politically feasible.

Increased tensions over trade could hinder cooperation on issues concerning global public goods. Taxes on revenue could also hinder (not yet profitable) entrants,[83] potentially leading to an unfavorable lock-in of the status quo. Finally, others worry that digital tax proposals do not properly model on whom the burdens are likely to fall.[84] However, if digital sales taxes are likely to be implemented anyway, then pressure to utilize the generated revenue to hedge against TAI risk is likely to be positive.

Self-Assessed Corporate Taxes

A common ownership self-assessed tax (COST) requires firms to price the value of their organizations at some level $X, which firms themselves decide upon. If a bidder offers $X for the firm, firms are required to sell. Firms pay taxes of 7% conditional on their chosen price (higher prices incur higher taxes).

COST should be implemented in areas where large firms have low risk of asset forfeiture (e.g. COST could be implemented in countries where Big Tech invests a relatively small proportion of their assets).

If COST is implemented, then firms will be less able to shift assets abroad. Consequently, tax evasion would be reduced, and revenue generated for the domestic country. The increased revenue generated from a COST could be invested into a SWF. Moreover, revenue would increase as firms become more valuable, meaning that countries have increasing payouts as AI firms become more powerful. This directly hedges against risks from unipolar outcomes, by providing countries with revenue as AI becomes increasingly important.

Although there are strong[85] objections to a widespread roll-out of COST, these mostly don't apply to a localized version of COST, where only firms (rather than individual households) are required to self-assess the value of their property.[86]

Appendix: Objections, FAQ

Objections

 

Won’t this speed up AI progress?

What if some countries do not allow ownership of their AI corporations?

Even if China does not allow that, countries can get exposure by buying the inputs to AI corporations from surrounding countries.

Diversification and Efficiency

If the AI sector collaborates more, it might become more efficient, and hence speed up AI progress. Even if diversification increases efficiency, diversification might decrease AI risk on net, as efficiency increases alongside shared mutual stakes such as safety. The effects of diversification on efficiency are ambiguous,[87] and we expect improvements in safety and capability to be intertwined in practice.[88] Overall, diversification should incentivise greater transparency, due to the larger number of shareholders to which firms are accountable.

Diversification may be anti-competitive, encouraging collusion as firms, acting for shareholders, prioritize maximizing the profits of the whole industry, rather than individual firm profits.[89] Empirically, some researchers find diversification decreases efficiency, while others do not [90],[91] and criticize theoretical measures to establish that diversification decreases efficiency.[92] Yet, others find that the association between common ownership and innovation inputs and outputs decreases with product market proximity and increases with technology proximity[93]

TAI and Power Dynamics

Greater diversification decentralizes power. If individuals or nation-states own larger stakes in AGI firms, TAI-conditional power will be more widely distributed. While multipolar power distributions risk coordination failures and conflict, unipolar outcomes pose equally serious risks like persistent global totalitarianism.[94] 

Our proposal for countries to invest in the global market portfolio could shift power dynamics by allowing nations trailing in AI development to catch up through returns from competitor investments. Though this might seem to increase competition risks, modeling suggests that competition actually intensifies when capability gaps are large.[95] By reducing these gaps, diversification could decrease multipolar competition risks.

Moreover, diversification creates credible incentives for cooperation on TAI policies. When nations hold stakes in each other's success, they become less pure competitors and more aligned stakeholders, offering a novel governance mechanism for multipolar cooperation.[96]

Incentives and Arms Races

Firms already have incentives to avoid misalignment, limiting diversification's benefits. The level of diversification needed to prevent arms races is unrealistic—even with 25% cross-ownership, firms would still race for AGI given the 3x advantage of winning.[97] 

And so, AGI is a prisoner's dilemma.[98] Even if firms want to cooperate on safety, they lack information about competitors' safety standards and ways to credibly commit. Diversification helps solve this: when firms know they share ownership, they can more credibly commit to cooperation. The shared stakes also incentivize transparency, potentially leading firms to share safety research. This research sharing could even reduce risks from TAI systems misidentifying each other, since systems trained on similar data would have more compatible world-models.  

Appendix: Uncertainties, Reservations, & Further Remarks

3.3. Does passive investment affect financial stability?

Passive investing can improve financial stability due to:

  1. Liquidity transformation and redemption.[99] 
  2. Diversification from passive investment also insures against shocks, and hedges against risks from 'pro-cyclical fund flows and redemptions during periods of financial stress'.[100] Intuitively, there is no incentive to chase performance and take risks when passively investing.[101]

Passive investing also increases financial volatility—through increased concentration due to incentives to buy minimally differentiated, lowest-cost funds by large asset management firms. This leads to operational problems at corporations (e.g. idiosyncratic shocks, such as cybersecurity breaches).[102]

Passive investing through ETFs amplifies the global financial cycle (GFC) in emerging markets.[103] One might worry that SWFs (which are suggesting invest passively) would increase global financial volatility.[104] When countries are exposed to the GFC, they have less monetary policy independence, at least without managing the capital account.[105] They are also more sensitive to the effects of US monetary policy, given its driving role in the GFC.[106]

However, the transmission of financial shocks may be reciprocal,[107] and reciprocal shocks could incentivise coordination on global macroeconomic policy. Moreover, even if international coordination could not eliminate the increased volatility occurring via exposure to the GFC, revenues from SWFs could be used to stabilize the economy after shocks.[108] While we acknowledge the risks from greater financial integration, we think that economies will, inevitably, end up being affected by the GFC. By implementing SWFs, countries can at least insure against unexpected shocks from the GFC.

Finally, more diversification in the banking system might increase 'systemic risk: though diversification decreases the chance of each bank's failure, it may increase the probability of joint failures'.[109]

Passive Investors and US Banks - Clark Center Forum 

3.6. Diversification and Great Power Conflicts

One large-scale global risk is the chance of a great power conflict[110] If two countries are warring, they are less likely to cooperate on (for example) issues of climate change or biosecurity.

Diversification increases the costs from war, as countries have more stake in their competitors. In addition, if the great powers of the future are more like firms than nation-states, then diversification offers one way of reducing risks from GPCs without relying on large international organizations, which might be unable to keep track of fast-paced technological development.[111] 

We note two possible criticisms of diversification from a GPC perspective. Firstly, diversification (by acting as insurance) improves the worst-case scenarios from war, which could incentivise war. Secondly, one might think increased diversification would increase the probability of bilateral conflict. This is because, with increased global interconnectedness, countries rely less on their local neighbors, and are marginally more incentivised to war with them.

On the first point, we think the marginal effect of making war less bad seems unlikely to counteract the benefits of increased cooperation. Even with insurance, wars are Very Bad. Secondly, although globalization plausibly increases the probability of bilateral conflicts between neighboring countries, it also decreases global conflicts.[112] This is for the same reason we might expect increased bilateral conflict: a more connected global economic system gives us more to lose from GPCs. Although we do not focus on GPCs, we expect diversification to reduce the probability of global wars, which are likely to be orders of magnitude worse in terms of human casualties.

3.7. Non-GDP Takeoff Metrics

Our SWF proposal involves a specific method of implementation: we suggest dividends from SWFs are distributed, conditional on either: a given firm's annual consolidated profits reaching 25% of gross world product (GWP), or a single country driving at least 50% of GWP. Others have argued against aggregate economic measures as a metric for TAI progress, as it is possible that we reach a 'point of no return' before we see large changes in GDP.[113] Some suggest that general purpose technologies which (perhaps drastically) increase growth in the long-run may decrease growth in the short-run.[114]

One might think that global GDP is an overly narrow metric from a longtermist lens, given the possibility of interstellar colonization, where individuating which actors have control over[115] The benefits of our proposal accrue under soft takeoff scenarios, where transformative economic impact is achieved before the development of AGI. Under such scenarios, we expect the international order to remain roughly stable

Although economic measures are easiest to implement, it is worth considering other commitment mechanisms. First, governments could commit to payout if some proportion (say 50%) of AGI researchers agree that one party has a decisive strategic advantage.[116] The relevant body of experts (or explicit criteria for picking experts) could be formed ahead of time. Alternatively, one might prefer to implement payouts when some fixed fraction of GWP is attributable to autonomous AI.[117] 

Finally, one might consider payouts conditional on a certain amount of funding being funneled into large AI research organizations, which could either be private firms of nation states. The amount of AI research funding could either be measured in absolute terms, or as a fraction of GDP/total running costs. If key actors start to accelerate funding into AI research, this is a sign that 'they have discovered ways to productively apply those funds', which is evidence that such organizations are facing an 'AI runway'.[118]

3.8. The Effects of Divestment

If divestment can have marginal effects,[119] then hedging against the worst-case scenarios may involve giving more resources to unsafe AI firms. Hedging would then mean self-interested or (in extreme cases) malevolent actors have more resources, which they could use to (e.g.) lobby governments more efficiently. Lobbying governments is particularly important in slow takeoff worlds (i.e., the worlds where our policy has the largest benefit).

Concerns about divestment do not apply to our case: we are suggesting a percentage investment in the global portfolio of equities. Ergo, our proposal should be expected to have relatively diffuse effects, although it will move wealth towards companies with a larger market cap.[120] 

Even if divestment did change share prices, such changes would be more likely to affect shareholders rather than usable capital.[121] Although we want to caution against investing in IPOs or SPOs to further prop up tech companies, we do not think that the arguments in favor of divestment are strong enough to counteract the aforementioned benefits of our proposal.

3.9. A Common Heritage Fund

It has been suggested that a common heritage fund (CHF) should be adopted, where total world trade is 'charged with a 1% import tax to be set aside for the establishment and operation' of the fund.[122] This fund would then be used to help preserve the future for later generations.

We prefer SWFs to CHFs for a number of reasons. First, SWFs are more tractable. CHFs would predominantly feature industrialized states as 'net payers', with 'the main beneficiaries' being developing states. Industrialized states have a greater financial incentive to create a SWF, making it more likely to be implemented than a CHF. Moreover, a CHF relies on enshrining a new proposal to existing international law, whereas our proposals incentive international cooperation without the need for large legislative changes.

Suggestions for CHFs focus on the preservation of natural resources.[123] Our SWF proposal is more general, and guards against a series of risks arising from technological advances, insufficient international cooperation, and other unexpected shocks.

3.10. Collaboration in a Diversified World

In the current world, firms maximize shareholder value (to the extent they do), because shareholders bring in capital, which firms will lose if they start undertaking actions which are not in the interest of shareholders. In a world where the majority of shareholders passively hold the global market portfolio, firms will be less incentivised to maximize shareholder value. This is because firms know that some investors will continue to passively hold the global market portfolio whatever they do. Therefore, firms can continue to think solely about profit, secure in the knowledge that investment from passive investors will remain as long as they maximize wealth. As we suggest SWFs auction off voting rights, one might think that our policies will not change firm incentives.

Our suggested policies will mitigate the extent to maximize shareholder value. However, firms operate under uncertainty, and may still be concerned about the possibility of nation-states (or individuals in the case of tax policies) threatening to move their portfolio allocation in response to firm actions.

Separately: states are less likely to engage in zero-sum 'races to the bottom' when their own investments are internationally diversified. This channel for increasing cooperation remains independently of firms' incentives to maximize shareholder value.

Overall, incentives towards cooperation and externality reduction are likely to be stronger for nation-states than firms. However, we think that diversification will still affect firm behavior. For instance, greater diversification could indirectly change firm behavior through national activity. The greater the degree to which a domestic country's assets are globally diversified, the larger the incentive to enforce regulation which disincentivizes zero-sum races to the bottom.

What policies are needed to respond to transformative AI? Here’s an Atlas to help you navigate them:

…Useful tool makes it intuitive to look at different policy responses to the AI revolution…

The Windfall Trust, a policy accelerator dedicated to dealing with the challenges to society posed by transformative AI, has published a “Windfall Policy Atlas” to make it intuitive to explore various policy proposals that “respond to the economic disruption from transformative AI”.

What kinds of ideas are in it? The atlas contains 48 distinct ideas, none of which are particularly novel. What makes it helpful is bucketing them into five distinct categories (public & social investments, labor market adaptation, wealth capture, regulation and market design, and global coordination), and then grouping these into a navigable interface that helps you explore them. For instance, “long term” solutions for labor might be shortened work weeks, while medium term ones might be workforce training and reskilling programs.

Why this matters - building intuitions for the world to come: As the AI revolution unfolds it’s critical we find ways to help people develop better intuitions about all the policy levers we could choose to pull to respond to it. Tools like this Atlas help make a complex, multi-faceted set of choices easier to visualize and navigate.

Read more: Windfall Policy Atlas (Windfall Trust website).

Anthropic Kickstarts Discussion On AI Economic Policy in DC

Anthropic hosted a convening of economists and policymakers in DC and gathered a broad range of policy proposals in an area where concrete ideas have been scarce so far. They categorized them from conventional to radical. While the former includes reskilling, tax reform, and the development of AI infrastructure, the latter encompasses AI adjustment mechanisms (similar to trade adjustment mechanisms) that assist displaced workers in moderate scenarios. Meanwhile, a sovereign wealth fund, additional value-added taxes, and new government revenue streams would address fast-moving scenarios. In response, Julian Jacobs (DeepMind) noted further ideas, such as unemployment insurance, the earned income tax credit, and a reward for contributions outside of formal employment.

The proposals represent a wide-ranging exploration rather than consensus recommendations, and the breadth of options discussed highlights just how early the field of AI economic policy is. The field has yet to develop any consensus on policy measures: instead, it is almost entirely at the stage of idea generation. Anthropic’s early actions in this uncharted territory are a first step towards opening a sizable can of worms that most researchers, much less policymakers, have yet to grapple with.

As a result, the BOJ’s purchases of ETFs since 2010 provide a unique opportunity. EPFR’s work complements Charoenwong, Morck, and Wiwattanakantang (2019), and Barbon and Gianinazzi (2019), which both conclude that ETF purchases made by the BOJ result in an increase in share prices and that the ‘BOJ premium’ does not revert in the short term. The research utilizes a stock-level fund allocation and flows dataset compiled by EPFR. The fund flows database, which covers mutual funds and Exchange-Traded Funds (ETF), contains as reported daily, weekly, and monthly data points from more than 18,000 equity funds and 9,300 bond funds from all domiciles. At the national level, encouraging some foreign asset holdings provides a form of macro-insurance: for example, a country with substantial foreign investments may fare better in a domestic crisis, since those external assets can be sold or will generate income to support the economy.

Sovereign wealth funds and public pension funds illustrate the insurance value of foreign investments. Clark and Monk (2010) note that governments use such funds to “promote long-term macroeconomic stability by separating a portion of national wealth from the domestic economy and placing it on international markets”econstor.eu

Drawbacks, risks, and reservations

High-income countries today face a fundamental policy trade-off: should national savings be invested more at home to spur domestic growth, or diversified internationally to reap higher returns and reduce risk? The “frontier” economies with aging populations and slowing productivity often see diminishing returns to additional capital at home, strengthening the case for international diversification. According to standard economic theory, as an economy converges to the technological frontier, the marginal product of capital falls, so investing in faster-growing foreign markets can yield a better risk-adjusted return. Empirical evidence supports this logic: small advanced economies with limited absorptive capacity (i.e. the ability to productively use additional capital) often experience diminishing returns and even asset bubbles if they force too much investment domesticallyeconstor.eu. One analysis notes that when countries accumulate reserves or surpluses far beyond what their home economy can absorb, investing the excess abroad is “rational,” since deploying it at home “can’t be efficiently invested…without asset bubbles and inflation”econstor.eu. This points to a clear benefit of diversification: it prevents the waste of surplus capital in low-yield or distortionary domestic projects.

Ultimately, research suggests an optimal balance: open economies should equalize the marginal productivity of capital at home with the risk-adjusted returns abroad. When domestic investment opportunities are abundant (or when external financing is hard to attract), policies tilting toward home investment may be growth-enhancing. Conversely, when domestic opportunities are scarce or capital is plentiful, encouraging global portfolios is welfare-improving. Over the long run, the free movement of capital can theoretically allow a win-win: domestic firms access foreign capital if local savers invest abroad, keeping domestic investment stable. In perfect capital markets, any home shortfall from local savers going abroad would be offset by foreign investors replacing the fundscnb.cz. In practice, market imperfections can make this adjustment incomplete, meaning excessive overseas investment could raise the cost of capital for home businesses if foreign investors don’t fully compensatecnb.cz. Thus, the trade-off requires careful calibration. High-income countries grappling with secular stagnation often pursue a dual approach: promoting some domestic investment (e.g. through public investment programs or incentives for local venture funding) while also allowing or even facilitating international diversification to maximize returns and spread risk. The literature underscores that neither autarkic home investment nor unfettered capital export is optimal—there is a need to support domestic capital formation and embrace global diversification in proportion to each country’s circumstances.

From a national economic perspective, does this home bias help or hurt economic outcomes? Correcting home bias (i.e. achieving more international diversification) is generally viewed as beneficial for investors’ risk-adjusted returns, but we must consider macroeconomic effects. Research indicates that reducing home bias can lower a country’s cost of capital and improve risk sharing across countries. For example, Lau et al. (2009) find that countries with higher home bias tend to have higher required returns for domestic firms: less global risk sharing means domestic investors demand a premium, raising the cost of capitalpapers.ssrn.com. In their study of 38 markets, the cost of equity capital is significantly lower in countries with more internationally diversified portfolios, implying that greater foreign participation in domestic markets (and vice versa) cuts financing costs and can stimulate investmentpapers.ssrn.com. Similarly, Sørensen et al. (2007) demonstrate that as home bias in equities and bonds declined in the late 1990s, international consumption risk-sharing improvedecb.europa.eu. Intuitively, when investors hold foreign assets, a nation’s residents are better insured against local economic shocks, smoothing consumption and incomeecb.europa.eu. This is a macroeconomic benefit: diversification allows countries to buffer against domestic recessions with returns from abroad.

On the other hand, could reducing home bias ever harm national outcomes? One theoretical concern is that if domestic investors shun home assets entirely, some local enterprises might face funding shortfalls if foreign investors do not step in. However, in globally integrated markets, that scenario is unlikely—capital tends to flow toward attractive investments regardless of origin. There is also an argument that during global crises, internationally diversified portfolios transmit foreign shocks (so highly globalized portfolios might fall in value simultaneously), whereas a home-biased portfolio might, by chance, evade a foreign crisis. But such diversification trade-offs are second-order compared to the substantial risk-reduction from not “putting all eggs in one (domestic) basket.” Overall, the consensus in the literature is that the home bias is an inefficiency: it forgoes significant risk reduction and potentially raises the cost of capital for local firmspapers.ssrn.com. Therefore, correcting this bias—through financial integration, investor education, and reduction of barriers—tends to improve national welfare. It may require countries to adjust in other ways (for instance, domestic firms must compete more globally for funds), but evidence so far suggests improved outcomes: more efficient capital allocation and better sharing of risk internationally. In short, home bias remains a puzzle and a suboptimal equilibrium; reducing it generally benefits the domestic economy via lower capital costs and greater financial stabilitypapers.ssrn.com.

Why not Mutual Diversification?

A separate approach might induce AI firms to undertake a contracted agreement to mutually invest in each other; this could either state that each firm has to own some percentage of their ‘rival’ firms, or invest some fixed fraction of their resources in a diversified AI portfolio.[140] Common ownership models have been growing in popularity: ‘the fraction of U.S. public firms held by institutional blockholders that simultaneously hold at least 5% of the common equity of other same-industry firms has increased from below 10% in 1980 to about 60% in 2014’.[141]

Mutual common ownership might enable firms to resist the effects of short-term market forces, and a competitive race to the bottom on safety. If AI development races take the form of a Prisoner’s Dilemma, then mutual common ownership offers one way of increasing trust between two competing parties, which increases the probability of cooperation.[142]

One downside of this proposal is that AI firms could aim to only benefit a narrow group (i.e., themselves). Even if we managed to get the incentives for safety right, there might be legal antitrust issues from mutual investment: some argue that investors in oligopolistic industries should only have control over one ‘effective firm’, or have a very small stake of the overall industry (<1%).[143] Worries about collusion and legal hurdles mean we are significantly less optimistic about this idea than a SWF.

Scale of the proposed funds

In 2012, the global market portfolio was around $90 trillion, of which around a third (36%) were equities.[144] As of 2017, the world's largest SWF in Norway owned 1.4% of global stocks.[145] We suggest sovereigns slowly phase in investment, starting at ~1% of the national budget,[146] until SWFs collectively own a third of the global market portfolio (SWFs currently hold $8 trillion in assets, but concentrated in just a few countries).[147] We suggest states collectively own a relatively large proportion of the market portfolio, as we expect AI ownership to become increasingly centralized.[148] By owning a large fraction of the global market, we decentralize power from TAI, in addition to increasing the incentives towards cooperation.[149] We expect that a wider adoption of SWFs will spread the benefits from TAI more widely, and provide countries with greater incentives to cooperate on an international scale.

Norway's present SWF/GDP ratio could not be adopted across the world, as Norway holds a disproportionate share of the global market (relative to both their population size and share of global GDP). Although we expect Norway's SWF/GDP ratio to decline over time,[150] more widespread adoption of SWFs would not result in a totally equitable distribution of power relative to population size. However, widespread SWF adoption would move the world towards a more equal distribution of power, and provide the aforementioned benefits from increased international cooperation.

Starting from levels similar to Norway's Pension Fund, until they own a third of the global market portfolio (SWFs currently hold $8 trillion in assets, but concentrated in just a few countries).[151] If unexpected downsides were noticed while slowly phasing in investment, investment levels should be reduced.

We are interested in distributing resources in a way that decreases the centralisation of power from AI. For this reason, we suggest tying payments to the relative market power of key actors, in order to ensure that the benefits get widely distributed, conditional on key actors having a large degree of relative power. We thus focus on %GWP, (which provides us with a measure of the fraction of the global output each entity controls), rather than global market cap, which provides a measure of absolute wealth. That said, we are aware that the metric is imperfect, as much of the world's economic activity occurs in contested states,[152] and we offer suggestions for alternate metrics in the appendix.

We suggest investing in SWFs at a level equal to the growth-rate of the global economy, with the rest distributed as dividends. Alternatively, the SWF could distribute dividends and buybacks, with the remainder reinvested. The numbers should be similar in either case, and diverge only to the extent that corporate earnings diverge from GDP.[153] Outside of AI-specific scenarios, dividend commitments based on relative GDP allows states to smooth domestic shocks.

We propose conditional dividend commitments to incentivise against premature liquidation, as rational politicians will know that money is more valuable during shocks that might occur while they are in office. To further alleviate public choice concerns, we propose that SWFs be run by independent central banks, so that short-sighted politicians cannot easily liquidate their assets. Conditional payouts also align incentives without bureaucracy.[154] Supervisory bodies might overreact to short-term trends and that 'in the long run everything will be fine' when it comes to short- term losses.[155] 

Based on national security concerns,[156] some have argued SWFs should only buy non-voting shares.[157] However, if countries simply purchased non-voting shares, then remaining privileged shareholders would get an undesirable subsidy.[158] To mitigate this concern, we suggest that countries buy voting shares, and then auction off the voting rights.[159]

More specific details on SWFs could be implemented. For example, a commitment to investing in the global portfolio could be included in the Santiago Principles (an international agreement on the best principles and practices of SWFs).[160]

3.4. Kinds of Longtermism

Our proposals should appeal to broad longtermists.[161] Greater diversification increases international cooperation, which is a plausible x-risk factor. Although we point out the benefits of diversification for AI, the benefits from common ownership apply more widely. SWFs, in particular, should appeal to patient longtermists. The more patient one is, the larger the benefit from accumulating resources with which to guard against large risks in the future.

3.5. SWFs and The Windfall Clause[162]

We believe SWFs are more promising than the windfall clause, which primarily incentivises signatories from altruistic companies. Thus, payouts occur if altruistic companies get ahead. In contrast, our proposal is more aligned with incentives of relevant actors, as we rely less heavily on altruism to create a social benefit. Because windfall clauses reduce a company's profits, signatories will (on average) receive less investment, and be less competitive than less altruistic non-signatories. SWF investment recoups dividends from non-altruistic, non-signatories. Hence, our proposal hedges more effectively against worst-case scenarios, and should therefore be preferred by those concerned with downside-risks.[163] 

SWFs are more promising than sovereign automation funds (SAF), a type of SWF that buys shares in AI firms. These funds might be seen to violate 'international norms against expropriation', because they try to gain control over AI firms' profits.[164] This would not be the case for passively run SWFs, which already exist and have large stakes in AI.[165] As we suggest auctioning off voting shares, there are fewer concerns about undue influence.

3.1. Will diversification lead to populism?

Despite the claimed benefits, our proposals are unlikely to offer a Pareto improvement. Greater diversification will likely harm some industries.[166] Indeed, some of the short-term harms (e.g., industry-specific wage reductions) may fall on low-wage workers, which could lead to a populist backlash.[167]

In the case of SWFs, we suggest that the distribution of dividends to low-income workers should be explicitly codified in the constitution of a SWF. This is to avoid situations where governments make promises to compensate the 'losers' of an increasingly globalized economy, which are then reneged on. Similar perverse incentives have been pointed out in the context of trade globalization: 'the winners need the losers' assent for the agreement. But once the agreement is passed, there is little reason for the winners to follow through'.[168] By engaging in some form of progressive redistribution, we hope to mitigate harms to low-income workers, and incentivise governments to maintain SWFs.

Replacing homeownership subsidies with opt-out tax cuts for internationally diversified pension plans is somewhat progressive by default. However, yet more progressive versions could be implemented. For instance, the counterfactual money freed up by investors opting out of tax cuts could be used to top up the pension plans of low-income workers.

At a pragmatic level, one might worry that our proposal seems unpatriotic. While we do not intend to provide a rhetorical defense of our policies, our preferred framing focuses on giving power to domestic countries. That is, one primary benefit is to ensure that individual countries get a fair share of the power from advanced technologies, without recourse to heavy-handed global governance regimes. The existence of global public goods (and bads) highlight the need for some form of global governance, and our policies are among the best ways of balancing tricky tradeoffs.[169] 

  1. Are SWFs worse than the Windfall clause and Other Voluntary Agreements?

There are many possible proposals for reaping the benefits from AI which are unlikely to merge endogenously through market forces.[170] Perhaps the most well-known proposal is the windfall clause, which we will examine first, before comparing our proposal to other possible voluntary agreements.  

  • New Sequence - Towards a worldwide, watertight Windfall Clause 

7.1 The Windfall Clause: Downside Risks

The windfall clause relies on voluntary signatories. In contrast, our proposal is more aligned with the financial incentives of relevant actors and does not have to rely on altruistic signatories for social benefit. Thus, our proposal hedges more effectively against worst-case scenarios, because only altruistic companies will sign up for the windfall clause, and so large payouts will only occur if altruistic companies get ahead.

Because windfall clauses reduce expected future profits of potential inventors, those companies will also receive less investment and be less competitive, compared less altruistic non-signatories, making worst-case scenarios more likely. Because the global market portfolio recoups dividends from non-altruistic, non-signatories, our proposal should be preferred by those concerned with downside-risks.[171] 

7.2 The Windfall Clause and Efficiency

In a previous section, we looked at the potential tradeoffs between increased diversification (a consequence of our proposal) and efficiency. The present evidence on diversification and efficiency is ambiguous. It will be instructive to compare our preferred proposal to the windfall clause, where the efficiency harms are likely to be greater.  

The windfall clause operates like a progressive corporate income tax,[172] for which the optimal rate is zero.[173] Our approach does not act like a corporate tax, and so does not have this drawback. Even if future research vindicates the existence of a diversification/efficiency tradeoff, current evidence favours our approach over the windfall clause in terms of efficiency. This is because (as discussed in Section 6) the case for believing that diversification hinders efficiency is not based on firm, well-motivated theory. On the other hand, the case for corporate taxes reducing innovation is, by comparison, much more well-founded. Thus, to the extent that one is concerned with efficiency, we believe that our proposal is more promising than the windfall clause.

That said, our approach is complementary to the windfall clause; our proposal bears some similarity to the ‘Global Wellbeing Windfall Fund’ (a suggested way of implementing the windfall) in the windfall paper,[174] except with less bureaucratic overhead, fewer possible legal issues, and no attempt to beat the market.

  • Only 33% that a major AI company will commit to a ‘windfall clause’ (see Import 181) by 2025.

7.3. Why Not a Sovereign Automation Fund?

In their paper on the windfall clause, O’Keefe et. al put forward the possibility of implementing a sovereign automation fund, for which they offer criticisms. We expand here on why our proposal is not vulnerable to their objections.

O’Keefe et. al (pg. 40) suggest implementing a sovereign automation fund (SAF), a type of SWF focused on acquiring shares of AI companies, and argue against this proposal. We now state how our approach differs. O’Keefe et. al worry about the possibility of corporations implementing  ‘poison pills’, to prevent the acquisition of ‘a significant voting share of the corporation’. This is not an issue under our proposal, as we recommend passive investment in the global portfolio. There is already precedent for this, as Norway’s[175] SWF invested many of its assets ‘in big technology stocks’. Our focus on a general SWF, run via passive investment, can help mitigate against the potential PR risks that might arise with a SAF, which could be seen as a mechanism for trying to gain explicit control over leading tech companies.

With global commitment to a SWF, we would enable a wide dispersal of benefits in all worlds where there are large monetary windfalls (though, benefits come from worlds in which there are TAI systems). Our proposal should not be seen as ‘a violation of international norms against expropriation’, as the tech sector is already a target of SWFs beyond just Norway,[176] a trend which seems relatively consistent across the past few years.[177],[178] For these reasons, we do not think the criticism offered by O’Keefe et. al undermines our specific proposal.

7.4. Mutual Diversification

A separate approach might induce AI firms to undertake a contracted agreement to mutually invest in each other; this could either state that each firm has to own some percentage of their ‘rival’ firms, or invest some fixed fraction of their resources in a diversified AI portfolio. Common ownership models have been growing in popularity: “the fraction of U.S. public firms held by institutional blockholders that simultaneously hold at least 5% of the common equity of other same-industry firms has increased from below 10% in 1980 to about 60% in 2014.[179]

One upside of mutual common ownership is its potential compatibility with firms’ long-term incentives, as greater collaboration might enable firms to resist the effects of short-term market forces, and a competitive race to the bottom on safety. If AI development races take the form of a Prisoner’s Dilemma, then mutual common ownership offers one way of increasing trust between two competing parties, which increases the probability of cooperation.[180]

The downside of this proposal is the potential for collusion: AI firms could aim to only benefit a narrow group (i.e., themselves). Even if we managed to get the incentives for safety right, there might be legal antitrust issues from mutual investment: in part due to the literature on the anti-competitive effects of diversification outlined in Section 6, Posner, Morton, and Weyl argue that there shouldn’t be legal scope for cross-firm investment. According to them, in oligopolistic industries, investors should only have control over one ‘effective firm’, or have a very small stake of the overall industry (<1%).[181] This is a significant downside of cross-ownership: the success of this proposal presents a potential legal hurdle that SWFs do not,[182][183][184] and is vulnerable to more conclusive future research showing harmful anti-competitive effects from diversification. Given that the potential efficiency downsides of mutual common ownership covary with the potential efficiency downsides of SWFs, in addition to a series of additional troubles (including potential legal issues), we are less optimistic about this idea than a SWF.

Will SWFs cause national security concerns?

We limit our suggestion to a small share of each country’s GDP, and (ideally) to the holding of non-voting shares. This helps mitigate possible national security concerns, which might arise if an influx of foreign investment by SWFs led home countries to believe that the purpose of the investment might be to secure control of strategically important industries for political (rather than financial) gain.

Increased international tension would, in expectation, be a large negative externality. It is unclear whether tension would arise in practice even if SWFs maintained voting shares, as “the majority of sovereign wealth funds” have their investments (both direct and indirect) spread globally (albeit with a US bias in venture capital, and a local bias generally).[185] This uncertainty is compounded by a series of further factors: mid-level powers may use SWFs to guard against external risk,[186] which may make our explicit focus on the use of SWFs to mitigate against downside risks seem more attractive to various nation states. Countries may also use SWFs to preserve their autonomy through the power of finance,[187] which would presumably decrease the probability of unipolar outcomes. While this is potentially positive for reducing the risks from global totalitarianism,[188] others have warned of the risks for multipolar outcomes in the context of TAI.[189] We currently believe that the increased chance of a multipolar outcome under our proposal does not exacerbate the risk of catastrophic coordination failures, as we think that there are independent reasons to believe our proposal will increase collaboration among AI firms, thereby decreasing the overall risk of cooperation failures.

Will SWFs be Intransparent?

  • Worries about Intransparency of SWFs. Probably not that big a deal, based on past empirical evidence; people mostly trust SWFs.[190]
  • Unfortunately, we believe that our approach is unlikely to be helpful in a fast takeoff scenario, as it’s not clear how we can use the resources we’ve garnered from mission hedging in a world where an AGI takes over relatively quickly.

Will SWFs be poorly managed?

We suggest that countries utilise external managers, and maintain a strong commitment to passive investment. In a comprehensive 2019 overview of SWFs, it is stated that ‘overall, SWFs are criticized for their poor governance and political motivations’.[191] We have already extolled the virtues of passive investment in the context of our proposal, but it may be worth looking at some empirical literature to emphasise the importance of this restriction.

Striking: “the coefficient on the politician dummy reflects a 41.3 percent increase in the likelihood of investing at home when politicians are involved. In comparison, the coefficient on the external manager dummy is equivalent to a 27.3 percent lower share of domestic investments when external managers are employed.”

  • History on the use of revenue from SWFs: Norway spent some judiciously, but invested a lot into dying industries, and ‘spent aggressively’, bringing ‘an unprecedented wave of bankruptcies’. Two other examples of imprudent spending after a huge influx of revenue are mentioned: the Netherlands in the 60s, and Spain after their overseas conquests (pg. 4 - 5). This just reinforces the first point, I think: SWFs should be conducted passively by an independent monetary authority.

A separate worry is that our proposal might involve financially aiding companies which bring about harmful effects, and thus that, on the margin, we do harm by helping such companies. Paul Christiano has argued that EAs have underrated the effects of divestment in the past.[192] If one buys the Christiano-style argument that divestment can have marginal effects, then hedging against the worst-case scenarios may involve giving more resources to unsafe AI firms, which means they can (e.g.) lobby governments more efficiently. Lobbying governments might be particularly important in slow takeoff worlds (i.e., the worlds where we actually expect hedging to be useful in risky scenarios), where the transition of power to AGI is continuous.

We do not think Christiano’s concerns about divestment applies to our case: we are suggesting a percentage investment in the global portfolio of equities, and hence our proposal should be expected to equally benefit all publicly traded companies. Moreover, even if divestment did change share prices, we think it unlikely that there would be a large marginal benefit to divestment, as we think that such changes would be more likely to affect shareholders rather than usable capital.[193] Although we want to caution against investing in IPOs or SPOs to further prop up tech companies, we do not think that the arguments in favour of divestment are strong enough to counteract the aforementioned benefits of our proposal.

  1. Diversification and Efficiency

Despite the benefits listed above, diversification might also have harmful anti-competitive effects like collusion.[194] 

Intuitively, diversification incentivises collusion.[195] Suppose shareholders have stakes in firms A and B, both of whom are jointly dominant in their respective market. There would be no competitive pressure to reduce prices to marginal cost. A and B may instead collude, and set their prices above marginal cost. If governments invest in an industry, they would be incentivised to strategically advise CEOs to raise prices, which increases the profits. This mitigates the benefits of competition on lowering prices.

However, the evidence of diversification increasing collusion is ambiguous:

  1. The original study showing this effect has failed to replicate [196],[197] 
  2. Others criticise the theoretical measures used to show diversification reduces efficiency,[198] 
  3. Common ownership does not predict increased profits well.[199]

But even if diversification decreased efficiency, the benefits might still outweigh the downsides.[200] Investing in the global market portfolio disincentivises supracompetitive pricing arising from collusion. Firms who maximise industry (rather than own-firm) profits would create a deadweight loss for complementary industries elsewhere in the global economy. Thus, countries are incentivised to reduce collusion, which reduces the overall value of their SWF. This would create novel incentives to combat anti-competitive behaviour.

  1. Does diversification reduce efficiency?

Large-shareholder diversification can have harmful anti-competitive effects.[201] 

Intuitively, diversification incentivises collusive behaviour: if shareholders have stakes in (say) two competing firms A and B, who are jointly dominant in their respective market, then there will be no competitive pressure on firms to reduce their prices equal to marginal cost. This is because A and B may collude with each other, and jointly set their prices above marginal cost.

More specifically, under our proposal, perhaps one worries that governments who invest in multiple competitors in an industry would be incentivised to strategically advise CEOs to raise prices on their products, as this will allow profits to increase across various competitors, mitigating the beneficial effects of competition on lowering prices.

Under stable financial systems, prices carry information, allowing for more efficient trades, thereby promoting economic growth.

  • A percentage point increase in unemployment lowers welfare by more than 5x as much as a percentage point increase in the inflation rate,[202] but this contradicts earlier studies,[203] and in any case ignores certain extreme events which might be important to include over a long time horizon, such as hyperinflation.
  • Potential depletion of the central bank reserves (see footnote 10 for the paper where a regression which finds the inverse effect)

6.1. Diversification and Efficiency: The Argument

The case against diversification is as follows:[204]

  • Premise 1: Because institutional investors are intra-industry diversified, they benefit if their portfolio firms seek to maximize industry, rather than own-firm, profits.
  • Premise 2: Corporate managers seek to maximize the returns of their corporations’ largest shareholders—intra-industry diversified institutional investors—and will thus pursue maximization of industry profits.
  • Premise 3: Industry profits, unlike own-firm profits, are maximized when producers refrain from underpricing their rivals to win business.

Ergo:

  • Conclusion: Intra-industry diversification by institutional investors reduces price competition.

Lambert argues against Premise 1 by noting that asset management firms which are intra-industry diversified are also inter-industry diversified. Maximising the profit of one industry causes extortionate pricing and harms other complementary industries.

They also argue against Premise 2, by pointing out that there are several reasons to doubt that corporate managers would neglect own-firm interests, including both legal issues, and the fact that the majority of the stock would still held by shareholders who are not intra-industry diversified (hence shareholder-pleasing corporate owners would still maximise own-firm profits).[205]

Evaluating their arguments in the context of our proposal thus requires both: (i) examining the empirical evidence used to support both premises, and (ii) adjudicating how generalisable such evidence on the behaviour of investors is to a world where we have implemented our suggested SWF. We examine both issues.

Impact investing in efficient equity markets

Impact investing in efficient equity markets

According to the efficient capital market hypothesis, asset prices fully reflect all available information, making it difficult for individual investors to achieve better risk-adjusted financial returns than the market.[206] If markets were efficient, then demand curve for stocks would be nearly horizontal (in technical terms, nearly perfectly elastic) because arbitrageurs would return stocks to fundamental values. If so, changes in demand have no effect on the stock price.[207]

There is a wealth of evidence demonstrating that capital markets have some inefficiencies over the course of around 3 months.[208] In other words, there is evidence that demand curves are downward sloping in the short-term. There is much less agreement on how efficient markets are on the >3-month timescale.[209] Petajisto (2011) writes of stock market demand curves:

'Today the evidence for downward-sloping demand curves in general is overwhelming. The main unsettled question is about how the slope depends on the horizon: if demand curves are much steeper in the short run than in the long run, then the price impact will reverse quickly…'[210]

The reason for this disagreement is that it is difficult to statistically assess the longer-term demand curve of stocks. Some recent work suggests that over the course of around 6 months, demand curves are nearly perfectly elastic, such that prices fully revert back over this timescale.[211] Other work also suggests that probably more than half of the effect reverses over the ~6 month timeframe.[212] However, there is also some evidence that price anomalies can persist for much longer than 6 months, suggestive of long-term inefficiency.[213]

Difficult to affect stock prices

This has interesting implications for impact investors working in large and liquid public stock markets. Assuming that stock markets are highly efficient on the ~6-month timeframe, if impact investors increase the price of a stock in the short-term, socially neutral investors will likely sell their shares at a premium until the shares partially or completely revert to the equilibrium price in the medium term. Conversely, if enough investors divest from socially harmful companies such that their share prices fall, the odds are that socially neutral investors will buy up the underpriced stock, thereby returning the stock to its equilibrium price in the medium term.[214] Unless socially neutral investors revise downward the net present value of the company's cash flows, the effect on the stock price will be either highly attenuated or completely nullified in the long-term.

Impact investing could have a more sustained effect on stock prices if there were a sufficient move in the market away from socially neutral investing and towards impact investing. It might be argued that if (say) harmful industries comprise 20% of global equities, then the tipping point would be when 80% of stocks are divested because at lower levels of divestment, socially neutral investors could always buy up the equity left by socially responsible investors.[215] However, this line of argument seems mistaken. First, the efficient capital market hypothesis states that current market prices reflect all available information; it does not say that each individual investor has the same view of the correct valuation. (In this way, the efficient market hypothesis works by a 'wisdom of crowds' effect.) This means that not all socially neutral investors would believe that divested stocks are incorrectly priced. So, it is more plausible to suppose that 40%-60% would think that they are incorrectly priced, meaning that the tipping point must be that 20%-40% of the market is socially responsible (assuming that 20% of industries are harmful).

Moreover, many of those who think the stock is incorrectly priced face restrictions on their portfolios and so may not be able to move in. Investors also would not borrow to invest in a divested stock because doing so would be risky and it is not plausible that investors would significantly change their risk preference.[216] Thus, as a rule of thumb, it seems reasonable that if harmful industries constitute 20% of global equities, around 20% of stocks would have to be divested to substantially affect the cost of capital for harmful industries.[217]

In many cases, this tipping point seems a long way off. Of the $40 trillion of assets under active management in the US, around $9 trillion is now labelled as 'socially responsible investing'.[218] However, it is difficult to know what proportion of 'socially responsible investing' is truly socially responsible. For example, Vanguard's socially responsible European Stock Fund includes British American Tobacco and Royal Dutch Shell.[219] This kind of misleading labelling seems fairly typical in the space.[220] The willingness to be strict seems limited. As Ansar et al note:

'Despite the huge interest in the media and a three-decade evolution only about 80 organisations and funds (out of a likely universe of over 1,000) have ever substantially divested from tobacco equity and even fewer from tobacco debt.'[221]

As of 2013, only $5 billion has been divested from tobacco. The market cap of Philip Morris alone is $140 billion.[222] Other harmful industries are also large enough to make mounting an effective impact investing campaign seem difficult. For example, the world's largest oil and gas companies had a market capitalisation of $4 trillion at the end of 2012.[223] Overall, the impact investing tipping point seems a long way away at present. Moreover, given the market cap of the targeted companies, unless an investor controls a very large amount of capital, their own direct effect on stock prices is likely to be small in the first place.

The evidence on the direct effect of socially responsible investment on stock prices is ambiguous. Most previous divestment campaigns, with targets including tobacco, alcohol, weapons, gambling, and companies in apartheid-era South Africa, had modest or zero direct effect on the stock price of targeted companies.[224] On the other hand, there is also evidence that 'sin stocks' – stocks of companies producing harmful products, such as tobacco and gambling – consistently outperform the market. Hong and Kacperczyk (2009) note that this could either be because socially responsible investment has had a long-term effect, or because of other features of these industries, such as that they face a greater risk of litigation.[225]

To conclude, regarding the question of whether short-run price effects are negated after around 6 months, the evidence is limited and ambiguous, and the experts disagree. However, on the basis of the evidence we do have, it seems likely that in most cases probably more than half of the price effect is negated on this timescale. Moreover, since few individual investors will be able to have a noticeable effect on stock prices in the first place, our view is that, for the vast majority of socially responsible impact investors, their own actions will have at best modest direct effect on stock prices in large and liquid stock markets.

[86] COST allows users to bundle their assets into one ‘thing’, and pay taxes on that thing (e.g., you can set your desired price for a pair of shoes, not just one individual shoe). However, COST doesn’t allow you to bundle items temporally. For instance, I might value a home more if I could have it until my youngest child graduates from high school. But, under COST, I can’t set a price for: ‘my house for 15 years, or not at all’, and then pay taxes on that (Fennell, 2018). Again, this objection doesn’t matter as much for our proposal, as, for the purposes of this paper, we only care about COST for firms, rather than private goods.
